A foreign national visiting India claims equality before law under Article 14 and freedom to practise a profession under Article 19(1)(g). Which statement correctly identifies the constitutional position?
options_en: Both guarantees are confined to Indian citizens.
Article 14 extends to the foreign national; Article 19(1)(g) is guaranteed to citizens.
Both guarantees extend to the foreign national on the same basis as to citizens.
Article 19(1)(g) extends to the foreign national, but Article 14 does not.

question_snapshot.stem_en: Citizen shareholders of a newspaper company show that State action directly impairs their own freedom of expression exercised through the newspaper. The State objects solely because they act through a company. Which assessment follows from Bennett Coleman?
options_en: Their own constitutional rights do not disappear merely because they associate through a company.
Incorporation automatically makes the company a citizen for every Article19 purpose.
Only the company may raise the issue; the affected citizens necessarily lose standing.
Any loss in the value of shares automatically establishes infringement of Article19(1)(a).

question_snapshot.stem_en: Which statement correctly describes the constitutional basis of freedom of the press in India?
options_en: It is protected solely by occupational freedom under Article 19(1)(g).
It is implicit in the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).
It is expressly enumerated as a separate freedom alongside speech in Article 19(1)(a).
It is a freedom exclusively of journalists, unavailable to other citizens under Article 19(1)(a).

question_snapshot.stem_en: A truthful commercial advertisement is challenged on the sole ground that profit-oriented communication cannot receive any protection as speech. Which response best reflects the constitutional position?
options_en: Commercial purpose alone removes all Article 19(1)(a)protection.
Every advertisement is immune from regulation once it contains a price.
Only political advertisements can qualify as speech.
Commercial speech can be protected under Article 19(1)(a), subject to the applicable constitutional restrictions.

question_snapshot.stem_en: Schoolchildren stand respectfully during the national anthem but do not sing because of a genuine conscientious religious belief. They show no disrespect and disrupt no proceedings. Which constitutional consideration is most directly relevant, as recognised in Bijoe Emmanuel?
options_en: Protection of speech, silence and conscience must be considered; non-singing alone is not identical to disrespect.
Article 25(1) protects only organised religious ceremonies and cannot protect a pupil’s conscientious silence.
Article 19(1)(a) protects the choice of spoken words but excludes a choice to remain silent.
Respect for the anthem requires singing in every case, even when the pupils stand respectfully without disruption.

options_en: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

1. The statutory right to vote was distinguished from freedom of voting as expression under Article 19(1)(a).
2. Secrecy protected an elector choosing no candidate as well as an elector choosing a candidate.
3. Choosing NOTA required public disclosure of the elector’s identity and choice.
Which statements are correct?

Which statements are correct?

In a State Assembly constituency, the final count is: candidate A—30,000 votes; candidate B—25,000 votes; NOTA—35,000 votes. They are the only contesting candidates, and no other legal impediment exists. Under the Election Commission’s consolidated NOTA instructions of July 2023, what follows?
options_en: A fresh election must automatically be held because NOTA leads.
Candidate A is declared elected as the highest-polling contesting candidate.
The seat remains vacant until NOTA falls below a candidate’s total.
Both candidates are automatically disqualified from contesting again.

question_snapshot.stem_en: Which statement best reflects Justice Mathew’s observations on the right to know in State of U.P. v. Raj Narain (1975)?
options_en: Every official document must be disclosed irrespective of genuine public-security concerns.
Routine official transactions are outside the public’s right to know merely because officials performed them.
Knowledge of public acts is linked to speech freedom, but the right is not absolute and genuine public-security interests matter.
The right to know exists only for elected legislators, rather than the public.

question_snapshot.stem_en: Which statement best explains the constitutional importance of a voter knowing a candidate’s background, as reaffirmed in PUCL (2013)?
options_en: Ballot secrecy requires all information about candidates to remain secret.
Information enables an informed electoral choice protected as expression under Article 19(1)(a).
Only political parties have a constitutional interest in candidate information.
Because voting is statutory, candidate information cannot concern any Fundamental Right.
